concepts.title: Covalent Bonding and Tetravalency of Carbon
concepts.definition: A chemical link formed by the mutual sharing of valence electron pairs between atoms to reach stable electronic configurations.
concepts.formula: Valence electrons shared = Total electrons required to complete octet or duplet
concepts.key_idea: Carbon shares four valence electrons to attain a stable octet, forming covalent bonds with weak intermolecular forces.
question_patterns: explain why carbon forms covalent bonds instead of ionic bonds
describe the nature of covalent bonding in methane
why do covalent compounds have low melting and boiling points
explain why carbon cannot form C4+ or C4- ions
what do you understand by covalent bonding and tetravalency of carbon

solution_steps.explain: Carbon has atomic number 6 with 4 valence electrons in its outer shell.

solution_steps.action: evaluate energy barrier for ion formation
solution_steps.explain: Gaining 4 electrons (C4-) is unstable due to nuclear charge imbalance, and losing 4 electrons (C4+) demands excessive ionisation energy.
Carbon shares four electrons with other atoms to complete its octet without forming ionic species.

concepts.title: Allotropes of Carbon
concepts.definition: Distinct structural modifications of carbon possessing the same chemical composition but remarkably differing physical arrangements.
concepts.formula: Allotropes: Diamond (3D tetrahedral lattice), Graphite (hexagonal sheets), Fullerenes (spherical cages such as C60)
concepts.key_idea: Different spatial bonding arrangements of carbon atoms produce wide variations in hardness, conductivity, and texture.
question_patterns: differentiate between diamond and graphite based on structure
explain why graphite conducts electricity while diamond does not
what are fullerenes and what is the structure of C60
how can synthetic diamonds be prepared
state two key points about allotropes of carbon

solution_steps.explain: In diamond, each carbon bonds to 4 other carbons tetrahedrally; in graphite, each bonds to 3 carbons in planar hexagonal layers.
Graphite contains delocalised electrons from its pi-bonding system capable of electrical conduction, which diamond lacks.
Diamond is the hardest natural substance due to its rigid 3D lattice, while graphite is soft and slippery because layers slide over each other; fullerenes form hollow cages.

concepts.title: Versatile Nature of Carbon: Catenation and Tetravalency
concepts.definition: The exceptional capacity of carbon to bind with other carbon atoms in continuous chains, branches, and rings, coupled with a valency of four.
concepts.formula: Number of bonds formed per carbon = 4
concepts.key_idea: Strong C-C bond stability and tetravalency allow carbon to produce an extraordinarily vast number of compounds.
question_patterns: what are the two unique properties of carbon leading to millions of compounds
define catenation and explain why it is most pronounced in carbon
why are carbon-carbon bonds exceptionally stable
describe versatile nature of carbon: catenation and tetravalency with an example
what do you understand by versatile nature of carbon: catenation and tetravalency

solution_steps.explain: Carbon atoms readily link together via covalent bonds into straight chains, branched frameworks, or cyclic rings.
Its small atomic radius enables the nucleus to tightly hold shared electron pairs, ensuring high thermodynamic stability.
The combination of catenation and tetravalency allows carbon to form millions of compounds with chains, branches, and rings of varying lengths.

concepts.definition: Hydrocarbons containing only single covalent bonds between carbon atoms, conforming to a defined open-chain stoichiometry.
concepts.key_idea: For an alkane with n carbon atoms, the number of hydrogens is 2n+2.

concepts.title: Molecular Formula of Unsaturated Hydrocarbons (Alkenes and Alkynes)
concepts.definition: Hydrocarbons possessing at least one double or triple bond between adjacent carbon atoms.
concepts.formula: Alkenes: H = 2 * n; Alkynes: H = 2 * n - 2
concepts.key_idea: Alkenes have double bonds with formula CnH2n; alkynes have triple bonds with formula CnH2n-2.

solution_steps.explain: Alkyne hydrogens equal 2*n minus 2 due to the triple bond, and its molar mass is 12*n + alkyne_h.

concepts.title: Structural Isomerism in Hydrocarbons
concepts.definition: Molecules that share the identical molecular formula while having different spatial skeletal connectivity of their carbon backbones.
concepts.formula: Structural Isomers = Compounds with identical molecular formula but distinct structural layouts
concepts.key_idea: Butane (C4H10) is the simplest alkane to show isomerism, having two distinct structural isomers.

concepts.key_idea: Members of a homologous series show identical chemical both properties and regular gradations in physical properties like boiling point.

concepts.title: IUPAC Nomenclature and Functional Groups
concepts.definition: Systematic naming of organic molecules using the longest carbon chain modified by characteristic prefixes and suffixes for functional groups.
concepts.formula: Systematic Name = Prefix (if any) + Root word + Primary suffix (ane/ene/yne) + Secondary suffix (ol/al/one/oic acid)
concepts.key_idea: Heteroatoms and specific functional groups (alcohol, aldehyde, ketone, carboxylic acid, halo) determine chemical identity.

concepts.title: Combustion, Oxidation, Addition, and Substitution Reactions
concepts.definition: Primary chemical transformations of hydrocarbons involving combustion to CO2 and H2O, catalytic oxidation to acids, addition across unsaturations, and halogen substitution.
concepts.formula: Combustion: CxHy + (x + y/4) O2 -> x CO2 + (y/2) H2O + heat; Addition: CnH2n + H2 ->[Ni] CnH2n+2
concepts.key_idea: Saturated hydrocarbons undergo substitution in light, whereas unsaturated hydrocarbons undergo catalytic addition.

concepts.title: Properties and Reactions of Ethanol
concepts.definition: A commercially vital alcohol that reacts with active metals to liberate hydrogen and undergoes dehydration with hot concentrated sulphuric acid to form ethene.
concepts.formula: 2 CH3CH2OH + 2 Na -> 2 CH3CH2ONa + H2; CH3CH2OH ->[hot conc H2SO4, 443 K] CH2=CH2 + H2O
concepts.key_idea: Ethanol is indeed oxidised by alkaline KMnO4 to ethanoic both acid and dehydrated by concentrated H2SO4 to ethene.

solution_steps.explain: Ethanol reacts with sodium at ambient temperatures or with concentrated H2SO4 at 443 K.
Sodium reaction gives sodium ethoxide and H2 gas; heating with conc. H2SO4 dehydrates ethanol to ethene.

concepts.title: Properties and Reactions of Ethanoic Acid
concepts.definition: A weak carboxylic acid that forms sweet-smelling esters with alcohols, reacts with bases to yield carboxylate salts, and releases CO2 with carbonates.
concepts.formula: CH3COOH + C2H5OH ->[acid] CH3COOC2H5 + H2O; CH3COOH + NaHCO3 -> CH3COONa + H2O + CO2
concepts.key_idea: Ethanoic acid undergoes esterification, saponification in reverse with base, and effervesces with metal carbonates releasing CO2.

concepts.title: Cleansing Action of Soaps and Detergents
concepts.definition: Amphiphilic molecules possessing a hydrophilic ionic head and a hydrophobic hydrocarbon tail that form spherical micelles to emulsify and dislodge oily dirt.
concepts.key_idea: Soap fails in hard water because of insoluble scum formation with Ca2+/Mg2+, while synthetic detergents remain soluble.
question_patterns: explain the mechanism of the cleaning action of soaps
why does micelle formation take place when soap is added to water
explain the formation of scum when hard water is treated with soap
why are detergents effective even in hard water
how does cleansing action of soaps and detergents work

solution_steps.explain: Soap molecules have an ionic hydrophilic head soluble in water and a hydrophobic hydrocarbon tail soluble in oil.
In water, tails cluster inward entrapping oily dirt while ionic heads remain on the outer surface interacting with water.
Emulsified droplets repel one another due to surface charge and are easily rinsed away by water.
